title: Aquafaba: what chickpea liquid is and how it works

seo.title: Aquafaba: what chickpea liquid is and how to use it
seo.meta_description: Aquafaba is chickpea cooking or canning liquid. Carbohydrates, proteins and other solids let it form foams, stabilize emulsions and thicken foods.
seo.search_intent: Understand what aquafaba is, why it foams, what it contains and how it can be used in cooking.

excerpt: Aquafaba is the water left after cooking chickpeas or the liquid in canned chickpeas. Proteins, starch and other carbohydrates leach into the water and give it foaming, emulsifying and thickening properties. A 2024 review reported roughly 2.03–2.59 g carbohydrate, 0.08–2.8 g protein and 0.07–0.1 g fat per 100 ml, with large variation among methods.
content_html:
The liquid in a can of chickpeas looks like a by-product, but it has unusual culinary behavior. Aquafaba is chickpea cooking water—homemade or canned—that is concentrated enough to form foams, emulsions and gels.

What moves from the chickpea into the water?

During soaking and cooking, small amounts of protein, starch, sugars and other soluble compounds leave the seed and remain in the liquid. That mixture of macromolecules makes aquafaba behave very differently from plain water.

Why can it whip like egg white?

Proteins and other compounds help stabilize bubbles created during whipping. Studies of commercial aquafaba show that it can produce stable foams and can also act as an emulsifier and thickener.

It is not chemically identical to egg white even when it can replace some of egg white's functions in a recipe.

What does aquafaba contain nutritionally?

A 2024 systematic review found wide variation. The aquafabas studied contained roughly 2.03–2.59 g carbohydrate, 0.08–2.8 g protein and 0.07–0.1 g fat per 100 ml.

The protein range is very broad because composition depends on chickpea variety, water-to-bean ratio, cooking time, pressure and final concentration. One nutrition number should not be assigned to every can.

Canned vs. homemade aquafaba

Canned liquid often has fairly useful concentration, and the review found higher foamability in canned aquafaba than in many homemade preparations. At home, overly dilute cooking water can be gently reduced to concentrate the solids.

What can you use it for?

  • Whipped meringues and mousses without egg.
  • Aerating cakes and batters.
  • Emulsifying mayonnaise-style sauces.
  • Adding body or thickening some preparations.

Do three tablespoons always equal one egg?

Recipes often use approximate tablespoon conversions, but aquafaba is not a standardized chemical replacement. Strength varies substantially between brands and batches. For delicate recipes, viscosity and whipping performance matter more than one fixed spoon conversion.

Sodium depends on the can

If the chickpeas were packed with added salt, some sodium remains in the liquid. Low-sodium canned chickpeas or homemade aquafaba give more control for sweet recipes or sodium-restricted diets.

The practical takeaway

Aquafaba is not just dirty chickpea water: it contains soluble solids that can stabilize air and fat. Concentration varies, so recipes sometimes need adjustment or gentle reduction until the liquid has the right viscosity.

faq.question: What exactly is aquafaba?
faq.answer: It is chickpea cooking or canning liquid containing proteins, carbohydrates and other compounds that moved out of the beans.

faq.question: Why does aquafaba whip?
faq.answer: Proteins, starch and other solids help create and stabilize bubbles during whipping.

faq.question: Is aquafaba high in protein?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. A review found roughly 0.08–2.8 g protein per 100 ml depending on preparation, making it much less predictable than whole chickpeas.
